title: Algorithms for the Ferromagnetic Potts Model on Expanders
authors: Charlie Carlson (University of Colorado Boulder, USA), Ewan Davies (Colorado State University, USA), Nicolas Fraiman (University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, USA), Alexandra Kolla (University of California, Santa Cruz, USA), Aditya Potukuchi (York University, Canada), Corrine Yap (Rutgers University, USA)
abstract: We give algorithms for approximating the partition function of the ferromagnetic Potts model on d-regular expanding graphs. We require much weaker expansion than in previous works; for example, the expansion exhibited by the hypercube suffices. The main improvements come from a significantly sharper analysis of standard polymer models, using extremal graph theory and applications of Karger's algorithm to counting cuts that may be of independent interest. It is #BIS-hard to approximate the partition function at low temperatures on bounded-degree graphs, so our algorithm can be seen as evidence that hard instances of #BIS are rare. We believe that these methods can shed more light on other important problems such as sub-exponential algorithms for approximate counting problems.

One of our key innovations, that is of independent interest,
is an upper bound on the number of sets in a d-regular
η-expander with a prescribed edge-boundary size b. This
is reminiscent of container theorems from extremal graph
theory that bound the number of independent sets in some
graph or hypergraph. The origin of container theorems can
be traced back to Kleitman and Winston [15], [16], but the
ideas were developed signiﬁcantly by Sapozhenko [17], [18]
who speciﬁcally studied independent sets in expander graphs
and the hypercube. Algorithmic applications of containers for
counting independent sets in bipartite graphs were recently
given by Jenssen and Perkins [19], also with Potukuchi [8].
The type of bound we need does not seem to relate closely to
an existing container theorem, so we prove the following novel
result using additional ideas from randomized algorithms.

B. An overview of techniques
Our algorithms follow from the cluster expansion for abstract polymer models, which was ﬁrst used to design sampling
algorithms for the Potts model by Helmuth, Perkins and
Regts [21]. The method has been studied intensively since,
including further works concerning the ferromagnetic Potts

Markov random ﬁelds. At a high level, the method proceeds
by transforming the partition function into a representation
that corresponds to an abstract but particularly well-studied
polymer model from statistical mechanics. The strength of
this approach lies in the fact that general conditions on
these models give a wealth of probabilistic and algorithmic
information. The speciﬁc polymer models we rely on have

Algorithmic applications of the cluster expansion originate
in [21], and for the ferromagnetic Potts model in particular
there are two works of note that establish algorithms at all
temperatures on subgraphs of the integer lattice Zd [13] and
on regular graphs with strong expansion [5]. These results rely
on large q, which is a substantial drawback, but in return the
approaches work for all temperatures. The focus of our work
is slightly different, and essentially we pay for working with
smaller q (and much weaker expansion) by accepting a small
gap in our techniques around the threshold βo .
Our main tool is the cluster expansion for abstract polymer
models, as in [4], [5], [13], [21] (and many more works), where
deterministic approximation algorithms for partition functions
follow from convergent cluster expansions by approximating a truncated series. See also Barvinok’s work (e.g. the
monograph [26]) which follows a similar series approximation
approach. A twist on the cluster expansion method originating
in [7] uses a Markov chain to sample from an abstract
polymer model. The approaches of [4], [7] were combined and
generalized in [6] to give algorithms for general spin systems
on bipartite expanders. We do not pursue Markov-chain based
sampling from polymer models here as the conditions required
in [6], [7], [27] (i.e. upper bounds on polymer weights) are
stronger than what we can guarantee with our current methods,
and we do not want to restrict our attention to bipartite graphs.
